children: Samsung Wallet USDC purchases are now powered by Stripe, giving eligible Galaxy users in the United States a way to buy the dollar-pegged stablecoin through a familiar mobile app.

In a November 5 announcement, Stripe said its Crypto Onramp supports purchases in the Samsung Wallet Stablecoin Account across 82 million compatible U.S. Galaxy devices. Customers can buy USDC using Samsung Pay, credit and debit cards, or ACH bank payments.

That figure describes the potential device footprint, rather than 82 million registered accounts or active stablecoin users. Stripe did not disclose customer numbers, purchase volumes or transaction activity in its announcement.
How Samsung Wallet USDC purchases work

Stripe said its onramp “handles identity verification, compliance, and fraud prevention” as part of the purchase. Samsung Pay is also now available to other businesses using Stripe’s Crypto Onramp, extending the payment option beyond Samsung’s own stablecoin account.

For consumers, the practical change is the entry point. Buying digital dollars through a wallet already on a phone could make the first transaction less intimidating than opening a separate crypto exchange account. The commercial opportunity rests on whether that easier start translates into repeat payments and transfers.
Samsung’s stablecoin rollout began before Stripe’s announcement

The November update follows Samsung’s October 7 announcement, which scheduled the feature’s launch for the final week of that month. Stripe’s news identifies the purchase infrastructure supporting that rollout.

“Sending money abroad should feel as convenient as using the wallet already on your phone,” said Woncheol Chai, Samsung’s executive vice president and head of its Digital Wallet Team, in the October announcement.

Samsung described transfers to compatible crypto wallets and eligible bank accounts in more than 60 countries, with bank recipients receiving local currency. It also identified Bastion as an infrastructure provider and Coinbase as the sub-custodian securing USDC through Coinbase Prime Vault.

Samsung says it charges no fee for USDC transfers to supported external wallets, although receiving services can apply their own charges and network conditions affect speed. Bank remittances have a different fee structure, varying by destination and amount, with costs and estimated delivery times displayed before confirmation.
Samsung listed future online and in-store stablecoin payments as possible additions. Those plans should be distinguished from the funding and transfer capabilities being offered now.
Who can use the Samsung Wallet Stablecoin Account?

According to Samsung’s current FAQ, users must be at least 18 and live in an eligible U.S. jurisdiction. New York residents are currently excluded. Compatible devices need Android 13 or later and enabled fingerprint authentication.
The account supports holding, sending and receiving USDC, international remittances and optional rewards. Dollar deposits are converted into USDC, with withdrawals converted back into dollars.

Samsung says the account “holds digital assets, not bank deposits.” Balances and rewards lack FDIC, NCUA and SIPC protection. There is no account-opening fee, but funding, withdrawal and transfer costs depend on the method and destination; other providers may levy separate charges.

These details matter when comparing the feature with existing payment services. Convenience alone does not establish that a particular transfer will be cheaper. The relevant comparison is the total amount paid by the sender against what arrives at the destination.
Why distribution matters for stablecoin adoption

USDC issuer Circle reported approximately $69.2 billion in circulation as of November 5. Circle says the token is backed by liquid cash and cash-equivalent reserves and is redeemable one-for-one for U.S. dollars.

On its reserve transparency page, Circle says reserves are held separately from its operating funds and that it publishes weekly reserve disclosures alongside issuance and redemption flows. A major accounting firm provides monthly assurance on reserve coverage. Those disclosures offer a way to examine the backing of the token independently of announcements about new wallet integrations, although they do not measure how widely any individual wallet is used.

That structure gives USDC a different purpose from assets such as Bitcoin: it is designed to track the dollar, rather than offer exposure to a rising cryptocurrency price. Reserve backing, however, is a separate question from the protections and terms of a consumer wallet account.

children: . Samsung’s integration provides a concrete example of that distribution strategy: put access to digital dollars where consumers already manage other payment tools.

The potential advantage extends beyond attracting existing crypto holders. A person looking to send money abroad may care more about the recipient’s payout, the fee and the delivery time than the blockchain used behind the scenes. A useful product has to satisfy those needs consistently.
The next test is usage

The rollout offers a substantial distribution channel, but its success will require evidence beyond device compatibility. Account activation, repeat transfers and transaction volumes would help show whether customers see lasting value in the service.

For now, Stripe’s involvement establishes how eligible Samsung users can fund their stablecoin accounts. The next milestone is whether those purchases become a routine part of moving money, rather than a feature customers try once and leave unused.

title: Samsung Wallet Adds USDC Purchases Through Stripe
